question.text: The figure below shows the variation of specific heat capacity (C) of a solid as a function of temperature (T). The temperature is increased continuously from 0 to 500 K at a constant rate. Ignoring any volume change, the following statement (s) is (are) correct to a reasonable approximation.

options.text: The rate at which heat is absorbed in the range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math> varies linearly with temperature T.

Heat absorbed in increasing the temperature from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math> is less than the heat required for increasing the temperature from<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>400</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>500</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math>.
There is no change in the rate of heat absorption in the range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>400</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>500</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math>.
The rate of heat absorption increases in the range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>300</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">K</mi></math>.

solution.text:
q  =  mCT
dq dt = mc dT dt
R = rate of absorption of heat = dq dt ∝ C
(i) in 0-100 K
The graph between (0-100 K) appears to be a straight line upto a reasonable approximation.
(ii) Δ q = mC Δ T  as C  is more in (400-500 K) then (0-100 K) so heat is increasing.
(iii) C remains constant so there no change in R  from (400-500 K)
(iv) C is increases so R is increases in range (200-300 K)
